articles.title: Safeguarding concerns, community costs and fireworks raised at Rochdale council meeting
articles.excerpt: Farooq Ahmed raised concerns about safeguarding powers, while Jordan Tarrant-Short questioned venue costs, fireworks, foster care and Warwick Mill at full council.
articles.content_html:
Concerns about the potential misuse of safeguarding powers, community venue charges and fireworks nuisance were raised during Rochdale’s full council meeting on Thursday, October 15.

Councillor Farooq Ahmed questioned how the council prevented staff from overstepping their authority, while Councillor Jordan Tarrant-Short pressed cabinet members on issues including foster-carer recruitment, Warwick Mill and access to community facilities.

Councillors also rejected a proposal to rescind the council’s climate emergency commitments and backed motions concerning energy costs in new homes, protecting pubs and condemning attacks on places of worship.

Concern over safeguarding powers

Ahmed stressed that protecting vulnerable adults and children must come first, but questioned whether safeguarding procedures could sometimes harm the people they were intended to protect.

He said some officers could overstep their authority, leaving service users and families feeling victimised. He suggested the term safeguarding could be abused and asked how the council ensured staff did not misuse their powers.

Councillor Shah Wazir said safeguarding should protect and support people without causing avoidable distress. He outlined expectations around involving residents in decisions, providing advocacy where required and reviewing complaints and practice.

Responding to Ahmed’s supplementary question, Wazir invited him to provide specific incidents and promised they would be examined. The mayor also encouraged Ahmed to report his concerns.

The exchange raised concerns about potential misuse; it did not establish that misconduct had occurred in any particular case.

Community groups facing venue costs

Tarrant-Short said community organisations had contacted him about hire charges at facilities managed by Your Trust, warning that costs could make their activities financially unsustainable.

He told the meeting that a local dance group had reported being quoted £11,000 for one evening at Heywood Civic Centre. The booking requirements and an explanation of that reported quotation were not established during the exchange.

He asked whether protections, concessions or community pricing policies could prevent voluntary organisations being priced out.

Councillor Sue Smith said reduced rates or room-hire waivers could be available where appropriate, but charges also had to cover staffing, technical support and other operating costs.

She asked him to send details so officers could investigate. Smith said she had helped groups reduce charges, sometimes through changes to booking dates or times, but did not announce a new borough-wide pricing policy.

Fireworks and stronger safeguards

Tarrant-Short raised residents’ concerns about fireworks being used throughout the year, describing distress to families, vulnerable people and pets.

He asked what action the council and partner agencies were taking, then pressed for lobbying for stronger regulation and enforcement powers.

Councillor Tricia Ayrton acknowledged the concerns and said she had been speaking with partner agencies about a coordinated response.

She also said the council’s three community bonfire events would use reduced-noise fireworks, accompanied by music and lights. In response to his request for stronger national action, she encouraged councillors to raise concerns with their MPs.

Recruiting and retaining foster carers

Tarrant-Short asked how the council would increase the number of local foster carers and provide enough family placements for vulnerable children.

Councillor Rachel Massey outlined work through the Greater Manchester fostering recruitment hub, alongside specialist fostering, training and support. She identified particular needs for carers supporting teenagers, sibling groups and children with disabilities.

In a supplementary question, Tarrant-Short congratulated the children’s services team before asking what recruitment targets would replace retiring carers and increase overall capacity.

Massey said recruitment strategies and targets existed, while stressing the importance of finding the right home for each child. She did not give a numerical recruitment target in that exchange.

Warwick Mill and local investment

Tarrant-Short asked whether Warwick Mill would be acquired through compulsory purchase.

Council leader Neil Emmott said the council had negotiated an agreement with the owner and that cabinet had approved exercising an option to purchase following due diligence.

Asked why decisive intervention had taken so long, Emmott pointed to private ownership and previous unsuccessful redevelopment proposals, saying the council was now taking action.

Tarrant-Short also called for more community events in Rochdale South, including his Balderstone and Kirkholt ward.

Later, he asked whether a previously discussed highways review meeting had taken place. Scrutiny chair Councillor Tom Besford said no date had yet been arranged and promised to follow it up with him.

Pub protections and council votes

Tarrant-Short formally moved an amendment to the pub-protection motion, which councillors approved unanimously. The amended motion subsequently passed, supporting action over restrictive covenants that can prevent former pubs reopening.

Councillors unanimously supported motions on reducing energy costs in new homes and condemning attacks on places of worship.

A proposal to rescind the council’s climate emergency commitments was defeated.

Source: Rochdale Borough Council full council webcast, 15 October 2026: https://rochdale.public-i.tv/core/portal/webcast_interactive/1133238

articles.title: Heywood and Middleton North MP Visits Redwood School’s Sixth Form at Phoenix Centre
articles.excerpt: Elsie Blundell, MP for Heywood and Middleton North, visited Redwood School’s sixth form at the Phoenix Centre to engage with students and staff about their educational initiatives.
articles.content_html:
Elsie Blundell, the Member of Parliament for Heywood and Middleton North, visited the Redwood School’s sixth form campus located at the Phoenix Centre in Heywood on October 15. During her visit, she interacted with learners and staff to understand their efforts in supporting young people with special educational needs and disabilities.

Ms Blundell praised the teaching team for their role in helping students build essential skills and confidence for education, adult life, and future employment. She expressed her pride in having such a facility within her constituency, stating, "I’m so proud to have this facility - and the learners and parents - in my constituency."

The visit included discussions about various lessons, including the importance of recycling. Ms Blundell also enjoyed a meal of soup during her time at the school, which she described as "delicious." She thanked the staff and students for their warm welcome and the valuable lessons shared during her visit.

In her reflections on the day, Ms Blundell commended the young people, parents, teachers, and support staff for their hard work, writing, "Well done again to the young people, parents, teachers and support staff." This visit highlights the ongoing commitment to enhancing educational opportunities for students with special needs in the Heywood area.

articles.title: Rochdale social worker Nneamaka Uti shortlisted for national award
articles.excerpt: Nneamaka Uti, who works in Rochdale Council’s adult care service, is a finalist in the Social Worker of the Year Awards, with winners announced on 22 October.
articles.content_html:
A social worker helping adults in Rochdale has been shortlisted for a national award recognising outstanding work in the profession.

Nneamaka Uti, who works in Rochdale Borough Council’s adult care service, is a finalist for Newly Qualified Adult Social Worker of the Year at the 2026 Social Worker of the Year Awards.

The winners will be announced on Thursday 22 October, at an awards reception in London. The organisers have confirmed that the afternoon event will run from 2pm to 5pm.

Councillor Shah Wazir, the council’s cabinet member for adult care, welcomed the recognition.

He said: “This is lovely and deserved recognition for Nneamaka and showcases Rochdale’s caring side at its very best. Following adult care’s good CQC rating this underlines the high-quality care and support the council is delivering for residents across the borough. Best of luck to Nneamaka at the awards ceremony.”

The council’s announcement links Nneamaka’s shortlisting with the adult care service’s good Care Quality Commission rating, highlighting the contribution of staff supporting residents across the borough.

Now marking their 20th anniversary, the Social Worker of the Year Awards recognise achievements across children’s and adult social work in England. This year, the organisers have named 64 finalists across 14 categories.

Nneamaka is one of six finalists in the newly qualified adult social worker category. The shortlist recognises practitioners at the beginning of their careers, giving Rochdale a representative among those in contention for national recognition.

Gold and silver award recipients will be announced at the October reception.

Rochdale Daily wishes Nneamaka the best of luck.

Sources: Rochdale Borough Council announcement supplied to Rochdale Daily; official shortlist: https://www.socialworkawards.com/news/social-worker-of-the-year-award-finalists-announced-2026/ Event details: https://www.socialworkawards.com/awards-night/award-faqs/

articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council Publishes Budget Report for 2026/27 to 2028/29
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has published its Budget Report and Medium Term Financial Strategy, outlining financial plans and priorities for the next three years.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has released its Budget Report and Medium Term Financial Strategy for the financial years 2026/27 to 2028/29. This document outlines the council's financial plans and priorities over the next three years.

The report details expected revenue and expenditure, aiming to ensure financial stability and effective service delivery within the borough. It is a crucial step in planning for the future amid ongoing economic challenges.

Local residents and stakeholders are encouraged to review the report, which is available on the council's official website. This transparency allows for community engagement and feedback on the proposed financial strategies.

The council will continue to assess its financial position and make adjustments as necessary, with further updates expected in future council meetings.

articles.title: FIVE YEARS LATER, A COURT SUMMONS: Rochdale residents report historic Council Tax demands as arrears reach £28.4m
articles.excerpt: Several residents tell Rochdale Daily they have received summonses for old Council Tax bills, including a 2021 account. With arrears reportedly £28.4m, we examine recovery rules, compare council finances, and list free debt help.
articles.content_html:
ROCHDALE DAILY INVESTIGATION | 12 OCTOBER 2026

Several residents have approached Rochdale Daily reporting that they have received court summonses over Council Tax bills from previous years. One account relates to a bill dating back to 2021 — approximately five years ago. These reports are residents' accounts; the paper has not independently examined the full Council Tax and court history for every case.

For households already struggling with essentials, an old demand coupled with court costs can create significant additional pressure. The issue raises questions about whether Rochdale Council has changed its approach to historic arrears, what notices were originally sent, how payments are allocated and what support is offered before enforcement.

ROCHDALE'S £28.4 MILLION COUNCIL TAX ARREARS

Government collection returns for 2025/26, as compiled by Council Tax Helpline, place Rochdale's total Council Tax arrears outstanding at around £28.4 million at 31 March 2026, including recovery-related costs — up approximately 12.7% over the year. This is not the amount owed by any individual and should not be divided among residents as if everybody owes it.

Rochdale Council's draft 2025/26 accounts use a different accounting measure. Their Council Tax debtor balance increased from £19.585 million at 31 March 2025 to £21.958 million at 31 March 2026. Those figures should not be added to the £28.4 million or treated as directly interchangeable; they reflect different financial reporting definitions.

Sources: government 2025/26 collection returns https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/collection-rates-for-council-tax-and-non-domestic-rates-in-england-2025-to-2026; authority comparison https://www.counciltaxhelpline.co.uk/research/council-tax-arrears/; council draft accounts, Note 15 https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s122950/Append.%201%20for%20Draft%20Statement%20of%20Accounts%20202526.pdf

CAN THE COUNCIL SUMMON SOMEONE FOR A 2021 BILL IN 2026?

Potentially, yes. Regulation 34(3) of the Council Tax (Administration and Enforcement) Regulations 1992 generally gives a council six years from the date the sum became due to bring proceedings for a liability order. A bill described as relating to 2021 is not automatically outside that period in October 2026; the precise demand and due dates matter.

A previously granted liability order changes the position, because subsequent enforcement is not necessarily subject to the same six-year limit for starting the original proceedings. Anyone disputing liability or the timetable needs their account history, copies of notices, and dates of any earlier court orders.

Source: Council Tax (Administration and Enforcement) Regulations 1992, Regulation 34 https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1992/613/regulation/34

WHAT ARE THE COURT COSTS — AND WHAT SHOULD YOU DO?

Rochdale Council's court-hearings guidance says a summons may carry court costs of £101.50 or £102. If the council obtains a liability order, enforcement fees may increase what someone has to pay. A summons is not proof that the amount claimed is accurate: residents can challenge liability or payment records through the proper process.

Residents should NOT ignore a summons. Ask immediately for the annual bill, statutory reminders, itemised transactions and credits, discounts and exemptions, dates notices were sent, and confirmation of whether a liability order already exists. If challenging liability before magistrates, follow the court-hearing telephone attendance instructions on Rochdale Council's website and the summons itself. Financial hardship alone is not normally a defence to liability, but it is a reason to seek an affordable arrangement and specialist debt advice without delay.

Source: Rochdale Council court-hearing guidance https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-tax/problems-paying-council-tax/3; contact Council Tax 0300 303 8870 or council.tax@rochdale.gov.uk

COULD PAYMENTS BE GOING TO DIFFERENT TAX YEARS?

Rochdale Council explains that its software normally allocates a payment matching a current-year instalment to the current year. A payment matching more than one such instalment can also be allocated to the current balance rather than old arrears. Other payments may go to the oldest debt. Residents seeking to pay arrears for a specific year are advised to tell the council explicitly which year's debt the payment is intended to reduce.

That does not establish an error in any resident's case, but it makes a full payment allocation history essential when a debt resurfaces years later.

Source: Rochdale Council, 'How payments are allocated' https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-tax/pay-council-tax

IS THIS A NEW HISTORIC-DEBT CRACKDOWN?

The public records do not prove that. The council was collecting older arrears before 2026. In October 2023 it reported collecting approximately £2.5 million in Council Tax arrears by the end of that August, about £400,000 more than in the comparable prior period.

To establish whether residents are receiving more summonses for old debts now, Rochdale Daily is seeking year-by-year summons figures broken down by the year of original liability, amounts claimed, recovery costs, cancelled summonses and changes in recovery policy. We have not found such a breakdown in publicly accessible reporting.

Source: Council meeting reports, October 2023 https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/g6401/Public%20reports%20pack%2018th-Oct-2023%2018.00%20Council.pdf?T=10

AND WHAT ABOUT THE £50 MILLION UPPERBANKS LOANS?

Rochdale Council's draft accounts show £50.309 million in contractual loans owing from council-owned companies associated with the Upperbanks hotel and residential development at 31 March 2026. During 2025/26 the loans accrued approximately £2.020 million in interest and recorded £132,000 in repayments. Their loan arrangements include payment holidays and other contractual conditions.

These are NOT unpaid household taxes and the size of a commercial loan balance does not, by itself, imply it is overdue or in default. Crucially, no evidence has been established connecting Upperbanks lending with the pursuit of old Council Tax bills. The legitimate point of comparison is whether the council makes its debt-management decisions transparent across both areas of public finance.

Source: Rochdale Council draft 2025/26 accounts, loan disclosure https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s122950/Append.%201%20for%20Draft%20Statement%20of%20Accounts%20202526.pdf

FREE HELP IF YOU CANNOT AFFORD YOUR COUNCIL TAX

StepChange Debt Charity: 0800 138 1111, free advice online at https://www.stepchange.org. Advisers can help prioritise Council Tax arrears, assess household finances, work with creditors and consider suitable debt solutions.

National Debtline: 0808 808 4000, https://nationaldebtline.org. Independent help with Council Tax, summonses, liability orders, enforcement agents and budgeting.

Citizens Advice Rochdale: 0808 278 7803. Rochdale advice sessions include Number One Riverside, Smith Street. Check current drop-in and outreach arrangements at https://www.citizensadvicesort.org.uk/offices/rochdale. Support includes benefits, housing, debt and practical assistance.

MoneyHelper: find free regulated debt advice and budgeting guidance at https://www.moneyhelper.org.uk/en/money-troubles/dealing-with-debt/debt-advice-locator.

Rochdale Council Tax team: 0300 303 8870, council.tax@rochdale.gov.uk, https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-tax. Request an itemised statement, challenge inaccurate liability through the prescribed route, discuss affordable payment arrangements and ask about Council Tax Support.

COUNCIL TAX REDUCTIONS AND EMERGENCY SUPPORT

Rochdale residents on low incomes may qualify for Council Tax Support. Single-person discounts, disability-related reductions and statutory exemptions can apply where conditions are met. The council also has a discretionary Council Tax discount policy under Section 13A of the Local Government Finance Act 1992 for certain exceptional circumstances. Ask the Revenues and Benefits team what evidence is required.

Source: Rochdale Council discretionary Council Tax policy, updated March 2026 https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/2426/discretionary-council-tax-discount-policy; Council Tax services https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-tax

Rochdale's Crisis and Resilience Fund supports eligible residents facing financial emergencies, including certain emergency payments, housing assistance and essential items. It does not automatically settle Council Tax arrears, but may relieve pressure on everyday essentials. Cost of Living Services: 01706 923685. Details at https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/cost-living/crisis-resilience-fund.

Some people can obtain a 'Breathing Space' debt respite through an authorised debt adviser. Standard Breathing Space can provide up to 60 days' protection from most enforcement action and interest or charges on qualifying debts, subject to eligibility. A separate scheme exists for qualifying mental health crisis treatment. It does not write off debts. Government guidance: https://www.gov.uk/options-for-dealing-with-your-debts/breathing-space.

SIX QUESTIONS FOR ROCHDALE COUNCIL

1. How many summonses issued in 2025 and 2026 related to Council Tax liabilities originating in 2021 or earlier?

2. Has any targeted exercise or policy change been introduced to recover older Council Tax debts, and when?

3. How much has been added to old balances through court and enforcement costs, and how much was actually collected?

4. How many summonses have been withdrawn because of incorrect liability, missing payment credits, defective notices or limitation issues?

5. What safeguards are used where residents disclose disability, serious illness, unemployment or acute financial hardship?

6. How many residents received repayment arrangements, Council Tax Support or exceptional discounts before enforcement progressed?

Rochdale Daily invites Rochdale Borough Council to respond with records and explanations. The paper also invites residents to share experiences of historic summonses confidentially at news@rochdaledaily.co.uk. Do not send personal financial reference numbers or identifiable court documents publicly; redact sensitive information before sharing.

THE BOTTOM LINE

Council Tax is a lawful obligation, and the council can pursue valid arrears. Residents are equally entitled to a clear statement of what they owe, when it became payable, which notices were served, how every payment was credited and what help is available if they cannot pay.

Rising arrears are documented. A new campaign of historic summonses, or a connection to Upperbanks, has not yet been demonstrated. Obtaining the age breakdown of court cases is the next test of the accounts residents have brought to Rochdale Daily.

General information only; individual debt cases require prompt, tailored advice and attention to any court deadline.

articles.title: Rochdale Council to Consider Motion to Reassess Climate Targets Amid Cost-of-Living Crisis
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council will discuss a motion from Cllr John Taylor on 13 October, urging a shift in focus from climate targets to addressing the cost-of-living crisis affecting residents.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council is set to discuss a motion on 13 October that calls for a reassessment of its climate emergency targets in light of the ongoing cost-of-living crisis. The motion, proposed by Councillor John Taylor, suggests that the council prioritise immediate support for residents over its commitment to environmental goals.

In 2019, the council declared a climate emergency and pledged to achieve carbon neutrality by 2038. However, Cllr Taylor argues that the local impact on carbon reduction has been minimal and that resources could be better allocated to address pressing economic challenges faced by the community.

The council meeting will also include updates on initiatives such as the expansion of the electric vehicle charging network and the Rochdale Town Centre Heat Network, which aims to utilise heat from sewers to reduce energy costs for buildings. The council has received a £1 million grant from the Government to support this project and will soon begin seeking a development partner.

As the council considers this motion, residents may be interested in how these discussions could influence future policies and support measures during the current economic climate.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Council called on to ‘scrap climate targets and focus on cost-of-living crisis’ - Rochdale Times Skip to content LATEST NEWS Council called on to ‘scrap climate targets and focus on cost-of-living crisis’ Rochdale Council is being called on to put helping residents during the cost-of-living crisis ahead of meeting environmental targets. When Rochdale’s full council meets on Thursday, it will consider a motion from Cllr John Taylor calling on the authority to rescind its commitment to climate emergency targets. The meeting will also hear updates on expanding the electric vehicle charging network and the Rochdale Town Centre Heat Network which will see heat from sewers beneath Rochdale will be harnessed to cut energy costs and keep buildings warm. The council has received a £1 million commercialisation grant from Government and will begin a tender for a development partner to take the scheme forward and prepare it for construction. Cllr Taylor’s motion reads: “In 2019 this council, in line with national trends, passed a climate emergency motion and committed resources (financial and human) to achieving carbon neutrality. “A key element of the motion was the inclusion of a Carbon Neutral Target which pledged to make both the council’s operations and the wider borough carbon neutral by 2038. “Since 2019 it has become clear that our local impact on carbon reduction is negligible and it does not represent the most efficient use of our resources. READ MORE: Heat from sewers will keep Rochdale warm in future “Consequently, it is appropriate to review our commitment to carbon neutrality and dispense with our 2019 pledge. “This council recognises the direct impact that the cost-of-living crisis and housing emergency have on many residents, and they must be our strategic priorities alongside the efficient and effective delivery of our core services. Future efforts to achieve carbon neutrality must also be cost neutral. “A local repeal will not override national legislation; the UK remains legally bound by the Climate Change Act to reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. “This is not a withdrawal from environmental action nor a belief that climate change is not a serious issue. It is a recognition of what is within our capacity to change and a renewed focus on deploying our controllable resources.” By rescinding the commitment to all climate emergency targets, Cllr Taylor hopes the council will direct resources to address the cost-of-living crisis and housing emergency. By reviewing all ongoing climate, carbon-neutrality activity, Cllr Taylor wants to stop any programmes that cannot demonstrate a “clear resident benefit, financial saving or statutory requirement”. articles.title: Construction begins on new banking hub at Morrisons in Heywood
articles.excerpt: Construction is under way on a new banking hub at the Morrisons site in Heywood, with Elsie Blundell MP saying the facility is expected to open by the end of October.
articles.content_html: Construction is under way on a new banking hub at the Morrisons site in Heywood, with fencing now in place around the new development. Elsie Blundell MP said she had met with Cash Access UK earlier this year to discuss bringing a banking hub to Heywood and has now welcomed the start of construction. The facility is being delivered as a modular building and is intended to provide banking services from the main banks in a shared location. It will be open to customers generally and will include improved access to cash. ### Expected opening Blundell said she had been told the banking hub should be open by the end of October. The new facility is being built in the car park at Morrisons in Heywood. Rochdale Daily will update this report if further confirmed information about the opening date and services becomes available. Source: Elsie Blundell MP. articles.content_html:
The Restore Britain Burnley & Hyndburn Branch has announced an evening event featuring guest speakers Charlie Downes and Montgomery Toms on Friday 16 October 2026.

According to the organisers, the event will take place from 7pm until 1am, with doors opening at 6.30pm.

The organisers say the evening will include speeches from Charlie Downes and Montgomery Toms, a light buffet and entertainment, alongside an opportunity for attendees to meet other members from across the North West.

Tickets are being sold by the organisers, with numbers described as limited.

The event is being promoted by the Restore Britain Burnley & Hyndburn Branch. Rochdale Daily has not independently verified the organisers’ ticket availability or other event arrangements.

articles.title: Birtle View Nursery opens at former Birtle site on Bury & Rochdale Old Road
articles.excerpt: Birtle View Nursery has opened at 239 Bury & Rochdale Old Road, with Mayor of Rochdale Councillor Faisal Rana attending the opening.
articles.content_html:
Birtle View Nursery has opened at 239 Bury & Rochdale Old Road in Heywood, with the Mayor of Rochdale, Councillor Faisal Rana, attending the opening.

Mayor Faisal Rana said he was pleased to visit the new nursery and described the transformation of the site as impressive. He said the nursery had created spaces intended to provide children and families with a welcoming, safe and supportive environment.

The mayor also met Councillor Paul Ellison, the councillor for the area, during the visit.

Birtle View Nursery is registered with Ofsted as a childcare setting providing full-day care. Ofsted records show the nursery was registered on 18 September 2026 and is currently listed as open. An inspection report has not yet been published.

The nursery is based at 239 Bury & Rochdale Old Road, Heywood, OL10 4BQ. The site has previously operated as the Bird I' Th' Hand premises.

The nursery's opening comes as new childcare provision is added in the area. Information published by the nursery indicates that it is intended for children aged from birth to five years.

Mayor Rana congratulated the team involved in bringing the nursery into operation and wished the nursery success.

Source: Office of the Mayor of Rochdale / Ofsted.

articles.title: Reform UK councillors reject proposed allowance increase
articles.excerpt: The Reform UK councillor group on Rochdale Borough Council has formally rejected a proposed increase in councillor allowances, with every group member notifying the council’s governance team that they will not accept any additional payout.
articles.content_html:
The Reform UK councillor group on Rochdale Borough Council has formally rejected a proposed increase in councillor allowances, with every group member notifying the council’s governance team that they will not accept any additional payout.

The controversial increase was rubber-stamped by Labour councillors present at the full council meeting on Thursday 16 July, with every single Labour member in attendance voting in favour. In contrast, Reform UK councillors voted unanimously against the motion, while other political groups on the council either abstained or voted against. At a time when local residents continue to face significant cost-of-living pressures and squeezed household budgets, the Reform UK group believes it is entirely wrong to increase politician payouts funded by the taxpayer. Each Reform UK councillor has now individually written to council officers to officially opt out of the increase, ensuring the extra funds remain in the public purse.

Speaking on behalf of the Reform UK group, Group Leader Councillor John Taylor said: "Hard-working families across Rochdale are having to make tough financial decisions every single day. The idea that local politicians should push through an increase in their own allowances—as Labour did at the full council meeting on 16 July—is completely out of touch with reality. We were elected to serve our community, not to line our own pockets. Reform UK voted against this increase in the chamber, and every single member of our group has now formally instructed council governance that we will refuse to take a single extra penny. We urge councillors from other parties to do the right thing and follow our lead." Reform UK remains committed to promoting financial responsibility, cutting waste in local government, and ensuring council resources are spent directly on frontline public services for the people of Rochdale.

articles.title: Rochdale MP Paul Waugh appointed education minister: what his new role means for the borough
articles.excerpt: Paul Waugh remains Rochdale's MP while taking on a second role as a junior education minister. We examine his responsibilities, additional salary and what the appointment could mean locally.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale MP Paul Waugh has joined the Government as a Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State in the Department for Education while continuing to represent the constituency in the House of Commons.

The appointment was formally confirmed as part of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's ministerial changes, with Mr Waugh taking up the post on 22 July 2026. Lucy Powell is the Secretary of State for Education and heads the department in which he will serve.

Mr Waugh now holds two connected public roles. He remains Rochdale's elected Member of Parliament, responsible for representing constituents, handling casework, holding surgeries, speaking on local issues and voting in the Commons. Alongside that work, he is now a junior government minister with responsibilities inside the Department for Education.

There is nothing unusual or constitutionally improper about an MP also serving as a minister. Most ministers in the House of Commons continue to represent their constituencies. His appointment does not create a vacancy, require a by-election or transfer his constituency responsibilities to another MP.

However, the ministerial job will substantially increase his workload. Ministers are expected to attend departmental meetings, study submissions from civil servants, help develop policy, answer parliamentary questions, take legislation through Parliament, meet education organisations and defend government decisions publicly.

That means constituents will reasonably expect reassurance that Rochdale casework and local representation will continue at the same level. Much of an MP's casework is managed by constituency and parliamentary staff, but Mr Waugh remains personally accountable to Rochdale voters and will still be expected to maintain a visible presence in the borough.

His precise policy portfolio has not yet been published by the Department for Education. The official government page currently confirms his rank and appointment but does not list a detailed set of responsibilities. It would therefore be premature to claim that he has direct control of a particular area such as schools, special educational needs, colleges or apprenticeships until the department formally allocates those duties.

As a Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, he is one of the department's junior ministers. Such ministers commonly oversee a defined group of policies, represent the department during Commons debates, answer written and oral questions, meet professional bodies and work under the direction of the Education Secretary and more senior ministers.

The Department for Education is responsible for education and children's services in England. Its work includes early years provision, schools, teacher recruitment and retention, the curriculum, children's social care, further education, higher education, apprenticeships and skills.

The appointment could give Rochdale a stronger connection to national education decision-making, although a minister is required to make decisions for the country as a whole rather than favouring their own constituency.

Locally, there are several areas where residents and education providers will watch his work closely. These include special educational needs and disabilities, school funding, teacher recruitment, attendance, college provision, apprenticeships and support for children requiring speech, language and communication services.

Mr Waugh has previously highlighted Rochdale's work on SEND and early speech and language support. In June, after hosting a ministerial visit to the borough, he said his job was to ensure Rochdale received every penny and every bit of support it had earned. His new position places him inside the department responsible for much of that national policy, although ministerial rules may limit how directly he can intervene in individual local funding decisions.

His salary is also expected to increase if he claims the ministerial salary attached to the post. All MPs currently receive a basic annual salary of £98,599. The claimed additional salary for a Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State serving in the Commons is £22,375.

That would produce total gross annual pay of £120,974 before tax, National Insurance and pension deductions. Ministerial salaries are separate from parliamentary expenses, which are intended to cover legitimate costs such as employing staff, running offices and travelling for parliamentary duties rather than providing additional personal income.

The increase is paid because ministerial office carries responsibilities beyond those of an ordinary backbench MP. Ministers are members of the Government and are bound by collective responsibility, meaning they are generally expected to support agreed government policy publicly or resign from office.

That obligation can occasionally create tension between the two roles. As Rochdale's MP, Mr Waugh is expected to raise local concerns and challenge decisions affecting his constituents. As a minister, he must also support the Government's education programme and comply with the Ministerial Code.

Having a minister as the local MP can provide greater access to senior figures and a deeper understanding of how government decisions are made. It does not, however, guarantee preferential funding or special treatment for the constituency. Decisions involving grants, schools and public bodies should continue to follow proper departmental processes.

Mr Waugh said he was "delighted" to be joining the Department for Education. His own website announced the appointment on 23 July, a day after the official government record says he took up the role.

The official announcement confirms that he joined an education team led by Lucy Powell, who became Education Secretary on 20 July. Other ministers in the department include Georgia Gould, Baroness Smith of Malvern and Josh MacAlister.

For Rochdale, the main test will be whether Mr Waugh can manage the demands of government while continuing to respond effectively to residents. Constituents should still contact his office about immigration cases, benefits, housing, public services and other matters requiring assistance from their MP.

His appointment raises Rochdale's profile within Westminster and places its MP closer to decisions affecting schools, children and skills across England. The title alone will not determine whether the borough benefits. That will depend on the responsibilities he is eventually given, the policies he helps deliver and whether residents continue to receive effective representation from their MP.

articles.title: Mayor praises Merhaba Festival as 'a wonderful celebration of community'
articles.excerpt: The Mayor of Rochdale has thanked organisers, volunteers and visitors following the Merhaba Festival, describing the event as 'a wonderful celebration of culture, community and togetherness'.
articles.content_html:
"What a fantastic day at the Merhaba Festival. As Mayor of Rochdale, and alongside the Mayoress, I was absolutely delighted to attend and see Rochdale Town Hall Square come alive with such a vibrant celebration of culture, community and togetherness.

There truly was something for everyone. From the delicious food and unique artisan stalls to the live entertainment and welcoming atmosphere, it was wonderful to see people of all ages and backgrounds coming together to enjoy such a special event. The smiles, the laughter and the incredible sense of community made for a truly memorable day.

Events like the Merhaba Festival showcase everything that is great about our borough. They provide an opportunity to learn about different cultures, support local businesses and community organisations, and strengthen the friendships that make Rochdale such a welcoming place to live.

I would like to offer my heartfelt thanks to all of the sponsors, partners and volunteers whose hard work and dedication made this festival possible. Events of this scale simply do not happen without the commitment of so many people working tirelessly behind the scenes. Your efforts have created an event that the whole borough can be proud of.

I also want to thank everyone who attended. Your enthusiasm, kindness and willingness to come together created a warm, welcoming and inclusive atmosphere throughout the day. It was inspiring to see families, friends and visitors enjoying everything the festival had to offer while celebrating the rich diversity that makes Rochdale so special.

As Mayor, I firmly believe Rochdale is at its very best when we celebrate our different cultures, support one another and come together as one community. The Merhaba Festival was a wonderful example of exactly that spirit.

There was great food, fantastic stalls, excellent entertainment and, above all, an amazing atmosphere that could be felt throughout the Town Hall Square from start to finish.

Thank you once again to everyone who helped make the Merhaba Festival such an outstanding success. I am already looking forward to seeing it return next year and to celebrating with our communities once again."

articles.title: Residents in Shawclough and Healey call for action over late-night fireworks
articles.excerpt: Residents in Shawclough and Healey are calling for stronger action after repeated late-night fireworks disrupted neighbourhoods, with concerns over sleep, vulnerable people, wildlife and the difficulty of identifying those responsible.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Shawclough and Healey are calling for stronger action after repeated late-night fireworks disturbed neighbourhoods, with many saying explosions after 11pm are affecting sleep, frightening children and causing distress to vulnerable people. While organised displays remain an important part of celebrations throughout the year, many residents say fireworks are increasingly being let off on ordinary evenings with little regard for those living nearby.

The latest complaints prompted a strong response on social media. Local resident Nick Simpson wrote: "Absolutely outrageous. These people need to be locked up and fined," reflecting frustration shared by others who say the disturbances have become an unwelcome feature of late evenings.

Councillor Shah Wazir also urged residents to report incidents wherever possible. Responding to complaints, he said: "Please report this to police and if you know the address then it will certainly help. Firework at night is totally unacceptable, no matter what occasion."

Fireworks are already regulated by law. In most circumstances they cannot legally be set off between 11pm and 7am, with later cut-off times applying only on Bonfire Night, New Year's Eve, Diwali and Chinese New Year. Retailers can only sell fireworks all year if they hold the appropriate licence, while most other retailers are restricted to seasonal sales.

Despite those laws, many residents believe enforcement remains one of the biggest challenges. Fireworks are usually set off after dark from private gardens, alleyways or open spaces, making it difficult for neighbours to identify exactly where they have come from. By the time officers could arrive, the noise has often stopped and those responsible may have left the area.

Many people are also understandably reluctant to confront those responsible themselves. Approaching unknown individuals late at night carries obvious risks, particularly where alcohol or antisocial behaviour may already be involved. Residents say they often feel they have little practical option beyond reporting incidents after they have happened, despite recognising that successful enforcement depends on accurate information.

The disruption extends far beyond a few loud bangs. Parents describe young children being startled awake and struggling to settle again, while elderly residents and people recovering from illness can lose valuable sleep. Mental health charities have also highlighted the impact unexpected fireworks can have on people living with anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder and other conditions where sudden loud noises may trigger distress.

Wildlife is also affected. Conservation organisations have warned that repeated fireworks can disturb nesting birds and protected species such as bats, while many pet owners report dogs, cats and other animals becoming frightened by sudden explosions. Unlike organised displays, fireworks used without warning leave residents with little opportunity to prepare vulnerable family members or animals.

The issue has prompted wider debate over whether existing laws go far enough or whether stronger enforcement is needed. While legislation already restricts when fireworks can be used, many residents argue the difficulty lies in identifying those responsible quickly enough for police to take effective action.

Greater Manchester Police encourages anyone witnessing the illegal use of fireworks or persistent antisocial behaviour to report it, particularly where an address or precise location can be provided. As concerns continue to emerge from Shawclough, Healey and other parts of the borough, many residents hope greater awareness, responsible use and more effective enforcement will help restore quieter evenings to Rochdale's neighbourhoods.

articles.title: One in Four: Why Greater Manchester Stayed Home
articles.excerpt: A record-low turnout of around 25.14 per cent has become one of the defining stories of Greater Manchester's mayoral by-election, raising fresh questions about voter engagement and the future of devolution.
articles.content_html:
The biggest story to emerge from Greater Manchester's mayoral by-election may not be who won, but who did not vote. With turnout reported at around 25.14 per cent, almost three quarters of eligible voters chose not to cast a ballot in an election that will determine who oversees policing, transport, housing, regeneration, skills funding and billions of pounds of public investment across the city-region.

The result represents the lowest turnout recorded since the office of Mayor of Greater Manchester was created in 2017. The inaugural mayoral election attracted around 28.9 per cent of eligible voters, participation increased to approximately 34.7 per cent in 2021 before easing to just over 32 per cent in 2024. Even allowing for the fact that by-elections traditionally attract fewer voters than scheduled elections, the latest figure has reignited debate about whether the region's devolved political system is truly engaging the public.

It is a striking contradiction. Over the past nine years the mayoralty has become significantly more powerful. The office now controls Transport for Greater Manchester, the Bee Network, policing through Police and Crime Commissioner powers, the Fire and Rescue Service, adult education funding, strategic planning and large parts of the region's regeneration programme. The mayor also acts as Greater Manchester's principal representative in negotiations with Westminster over devolution and investment.

Despite those responsibilities, many residents appear to remain unclear about exactly what the mayor does. Throughout the campaign, local news outlets, community groups and social media users encountered comments from voters asking whether the mayor controlled local councils, council tax or national government policy. That confusion suggests there remains a considerable gap between the powers exercised by the office and public understanding of those powers.

Several factors are likely to have contributed to the record-low turnout. First, this was a by-election rather than a scheduled mayoral contest. By-elections almost always produce lower participation because they lack the wider publicity generated by a general election or a full round of local elections. Without national party leaders dominating television debates and newspaper headlines, many casual voters simply pay less attention.

Timing may also have played a part. Polling took place during the school summer holidays, when many families were travelling or focused on other priorities. While postal voting allows people to participate away from home, elections held during holiday periods have historically struggled to match turnout achieved during spring or autumn campaigns.

Political fatigue is another possible explanation. Since 2024, voters have been asked to participate in multiple elections at different levels of government. Some political scientists argue that frequent elections can reduce participation over time, particularly where people feel they are repeatedly being asked to vote without seeing immediate improvements in their daily lives.

The departure of Andy Burnham also changed the character of the election. During his nine years as mayor, Burnham became one of the country's best-known regional politicians, often appearing on national television while leading campaigns on transport, homelessness, devolution and Greater Manchester's response to the Covid-19 pandemic. Whether voters agreed with him or not, his public profile undoubtedly helped define the office. This by-election was the first opportunity for voters to choose a successor rather than simply judge Burnham's record.

Campaign visibility became another talking point. While candidates visited communities across the ten Greater Manchester boroughs, many residents commented online that they had seen little evidence of campaigning compared with previous elections. Others said they only became aware of polling day shortly before voting opened. Those comments are anecdotal and should not be taken as representative of the wider electorate, but they echo criticism that metro mayoral elections still struggle to capture public attention despite the growing importance of the role.

The campaign itself was also unusually fragmented. Seven candidates contested the election, offering markedly different visions for Greater Manchester. Labour sought to build on Andy Burnham's legacy of transport integration and devolution. Reform UK focused heavily on crime, public spending and accountability. Restore Britain campaigned on transparency and local democracy, while the Conservatives, Greens, Liberal Democrats and independent candidate each promoted distinct policy priorities. Yet despite this broad choice, turnout remained stubbornly low.

For Rochdale residents, the result matters regardless of party politics. The mayor will influence transport investment affecting the borough, oversee policing priorities through Greater Manchester Police, support regeneration funding, negotiate future devolution settlements and help shape long-term economic strategy. Decisions made by the combined authority often have direct consequences for local services and infrastructure.

Some observers have argued that the low turnout should serve as a warning rather than simply another election statistic. Devolution was designed to bring political decision-making closer to local communities. If only one in four voters participates in choosing the person leading that process, questions inevitably arise about democratic legitimacy and public engagement.

There are no easy answers. Better civic education, clearer communication about the mayor's responsibilities, greater local media coverage and more visible campaigning have all been suggested as ways of increasing participation in future elections. Others believe turnout will naturally recover once the new mayor establishes a public profile and begins making decisions that directly affect residents across the region.

Whatever the explanation, one conclusion appears difficult to avoid. Greater Manchester now possesses one of the most powerful devolved political offices in England, yet public participation has moved in the opposite direction. Whoever occupies the mayor's office over the coming years faces a challenge extending beyond transport, housing or policing: rebuilding public confidence in local democracy itself.
